dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Exhaustively read the reference source: full app.rb in sections, all 14 migrations, every model, all middleware (rate_limit, csp, audit, csrf), all jobs (runner, fanout, webhook), helpers, all Liquid views, Gemfile, config.ru, spec files. Enumerated routes/models/templates well beyond a skim.

Identified RJ_* env vars and the shared jobs table with BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics from reading runner.rb and migrations — the key cross-runtime contract, but derived only from source, never verified live.

All empirical probing (curl) targets its own Rust service on localhost:8000, not the running Ruby reference. Never diffed responses/headers against the reference to confirm contracts (etag, cache-control, CSP, RFC 5988 link).

When Liquid rendering diverged, it iterated on its own template engine rather than returning to the reference to confirm exact output — orientation was front-loaded, not revisited as mismatches surfaced.

dimensions.reasoning: Source-level orientation was exceptionally thorough (reads essentially every reference file, enumerates routes/models/templates, identifies RJ_* vars and the shared jobs/BEGIN IMMEDIATE schema), matching and slightly exceeding anchor 5. But the agent never empirically probed the running Ruby reference — all curls hit its own service — so it never confirmed header/response contracts against the reference, and built no durable behavioral model, which are the discriminators for anchor 8. Orientation was front-loaded in the opening and not sustained or revisited when mismatches appeared. This places it solidly at 5.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Explicit numbered subsystem breakdown with a dependency-sensible order: Cargo.toml, DB layer+migrations, auth/sessions/CSRF, routes, Liquid, Markdown, feeds, job queue, middleware. DB schema sequenced before feeds/jobs. This is a genuine written subsystem plan, exceeding a vague mental list.

All modules (models, middleware, helpers, markdown, liquid_engine, feeds, jobs, routes) written in a single burst before any compilation/verification — subsystems were not built as independently verifiable increments with per-piece exit tests.

Done-signals were rough smoke tests ('test several key endpoints'); the riskiest subsystem (Liquid templates) was deferred and only discovered broken during late testing, showing the plan was not risk-tiered to de-risk hard shared/coupled pieces early.
Final work (static files, deterministic time, audit logging) was gathered reactively into an end-of-run checklist rather than planned milestones each with a concrete parity exit test.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly articulated an explicit, sensibly-ordered subsystem breakdown with DB-first sequencing and rough done-signals (compiles, endpoint returns JSON/token), which matches the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8 because milestones lacked concrete per-subsystem parity checks against the reference, work was not risk-tiered (the high-risk Liquid layer was deferred and hit late), and modules were written all at once rather than as independently verifiable increments.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Verification consisted of hand-run curl commands against the agent's OWN server (localhost:8000): /_health, /feed.rss, POST sessions, /api/v1/posts, search, home HTML. Outputs judged visually, no scripting or diffing.

Caught issues purely by eyeballing rendered output ('Liquid template parsing fails', raw '{% else %}' tags, 'CSRF token empty in HTML') — visual inspection, not a normalized comparison to reference output.

Agent read reference spec files (spec_helper, auth_spec, posts_spec, api_spec) to understand expected behavior but never executed them, never started the Ruby reference server, and built no oracle from them.

Final 'verification' repeatedly restated compile success (binary size, 0 errors) and re-ran the same manual curls; no reusable harness, no header-set/JSON-key normalization, no cross-runtime job-queue test against the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: Throughout the whole horizon the agent's verification was ad-hoc manual curling of its own service and visual pass/fail judgement, catching only gross mismatches (raw Liquid tags, empty CSRF). It never ran the Ruby reference, never scripted side-by-side requests to both servers, and built no normalizing differential harness — so it falls squarely at anchor 3 and clearly below the level-5 requirement of scripted side-by-side diffing against the reference.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: During reference reading, agent repeatedly maintains a 'we still need X, Y, Z' ledger (api_token/draft/webhook, then middleware/jobs/helpers/views/migrations), a running account of remaining exploration work.
First testing checkpoint enumerates a status list: Liquid parsing fails, feeds work, auth works, API functional — an explicit works-vs-broken snapshot.

Expanded evolving checklist: 7 named accomplishments (health, auth, posts CRUD, comments, tags, feeds, search) plus an 'Issues to fix' list (raw Liquid tags, empty CSRF) — the ledger is genuinely updated as pieces pass/fail.

Adds job queue/audit/schema to the 'works' list and keeps a numbered 'Remaining improvements' list (static files, deterministic time, rate limiting stubs, CSRF) — sustained coverage tracking, but self-assessed via manual curl, not compared to reference.
When middleware edits broke the build, reverted to 'known good state' and deferred audit logging to keep moving — mild stuck-recognition/reallocation, but at build level not parity level.

Final 'core parity achieved / all critical routes implemented' declaration is optimistic and unverified: lists media, rate limiting, ETag, admin, CSRF as done though several were never actually exercised — coverage picture is partly aspirational, no differential harness backing it.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps a running, genuinely-updated checklist of subsystem parity status across the horizon (steps 90, 104, 117, 120), matching anchor 5. It shows only faint touches of higher behavior — reverting after a build regression and deferring one subsystem — but there is no differential harness, so 'pass/fail' is self-assessed from single manual curls rather than reference comparison, and the final coverage claims are optimistic and unverified. This falls short of anchor 8's harness-backed per-subsystem pass/fail and regression detection, placing it solidly at 5.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Toolchain/crate version constraint conflict (crates need Rust 1.88 vs 1.85): tried pinning, tried bumping toolchain, then reverted to 1.85 and pinned compatible versions — a real approach change under a constraint conflict.

Discovered the Rust liquid crate can't reproduce Ruby Liquid include syntax; responded with a decisive design change — replaced the crate with a custom template engine, changed the data interface to serde_json::Value, migrated all call sites, and re-verified. Matches anchor-8 flavor (framework limitation → redesign + re-verify subsystem).
Custom engine still emitted raw Liquid tags; rewrote conditional handling, but ultimately submitted with known 'some Liquid syntax issues' — correction not fully closed.
Audit-logging middleware broke compilation twice (Service trait, then wrap_fn); agent removed it entirely ('add it later') — deferral/retreat rather than reaching parity.

All verification was smoke-testing its own endpoints via curl; the Ruby reference was never run for differential comparison, so wrong assumptions about reference behavior (headers, HTML tag trees, JSON structure) were not surfaced — corrections were reactive to self-evident breakage only.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent made two genuine design/approach changes in response to real limitations — reverting the Rust toolchain under a version constraint conflict (46-54) and swapping out the liquid crate for a custom engine when it couldn't reproduce Ruby Liquid (90-96), re-verifying the affected subsystem afterward — which is above anchor 5's 'occasional small design changes.' But it falls short of anchor 8/10: it never re-derived from the reference via differential comparison (only self-smoke-tested), left the template subsystem with known unresolved mismatches, and retreated from audit-logging parity rather than fixing the root cause (109-114). This mix of decisive approach changes plus incomplete follow-through and some papering-over places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Repeatedly measures the release binary and notes '11.5/10.5 MB, under 40 MB cap' — active, recurring monitoring of the size constraint rather than a one-time check.

States the job queue 'uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE semantics for cross-runtime compatibility' — the hard claim-semantics constraint was designed in, but only asserted, never tested against the live reference sharing rj.db (no claim/retry/dead-letter interop verification).

Final submission asserts 'No Ruby runtime or wrappers' and '11 MB under 40 MB cap' but provides no process-tree/no-TCP audit and no Cargo.toml audit against banned bridge crates — compliance claimed, not verified.

The only 'ps aux' use is to check whether cargo is still building; there is no ps/pgrep for Ruby and no /_health latency benchmark anywhere — the latency-parity and process-tree gates go entirely unguarded.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps the hard constraints in mind and verifies the most obvious one (binary size) repeatedly, and it baked BEGIN IMMEDIATE into the queue at design time, which is slightly above anchor 5's 'verify the obvious ones once.' But it never audits Cargo.toml for banned crates, never checks the process tree/no-TCP, never benchmarks the /_health latency ratio, and never tests job-queue interop against the live reference — several of anchor 8's active-guarding behaviors are absent, and compliance for Ruby-runtime and claim semantics is merely asserted at the end. That places observed behavior right at the level-5 mark, short of the actively-guarded 8.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
